walkthroughs.body_html: Durkheim (1893) argued some crime is inevitable and even functional: it reinforces boundaries (public outrage clarifies norms), enables social change (today's deviance is tomorrow's reform — e.g. suffragettes), acts as a safety valve and signals system failure. Too much crime is dysfunctional — anomie.

Merton (1938) argued American Dream values produce strain: not all have legitimate means to wealth. People respond via five modes of adaptation: conformity (most), innovation (criminal shortcuts), ritualism (giving up on goals), retreatism (dropouts) and rebellion (counter-culture).

Durkheim doesn't say how much crime is functional. Merton ignores non-utilitarian crime — vandalism for fun. Both ignore power: who defines norms? Marxists say law serves capitalist interests; feminists note male bias. Still, strain theory inspires modern subcultural theory.

mcqs.q: What is Merton's strain theory of crime?
options: Crime results from a mismatch between cultural goals (success, wealth) and legitimate means of achieving them — those who can't access legitimate means may innovate (crime), ritualise, retreat or rebel.
Strain theory says people commit crime because they are stressed.
It is treated more harshly than street crime.
Strain theory says criminals have psychological strain disorders.

Because criminals provide a useful service.
